Wedding Thank-You Notes: Wording and Timeline
What to write in a wedding thank-you card, how to mention a cash gift without naming the amount, and a realistic sending timeline.
Wedding Thank-You Note Guide
A good thank-you says what the gift was, how it will be used, and one warm sentence about seeing the person at the wedding. Three sentences is enough.
Timeline
Send within three months; earlier for gifts received before the day
Length
Three to four sentences, handwritten where possible
Cash gifts
Name the purpose, never the amount
Both partners
Sign jointly, or write from one voice and mention the other

Use a repeatable frame: thank them for the specific item, say where it will live or how it will be used, then add a personal line about the wedding. For a group gift, address the note to one person but name the group. Keep a spreadsheet of gift, giver, date received and date sent — it prevents the duplicate and omitted notes that couples regret most.

In the US registries are common and notes often reference the specific registered item; cash or cheque gifts are also frequent. UK and European guests more often give cash or a cheque, so wording around 'towards our first home' is useful. In many Asian wedding cultures money is given in a red envelope or ceremonial envelope at the event, and families may record givers separately — keep those records with your own list.

Do not use a printed insert, a generic message, or 'thank you for your generous gift' alone. Do not mention an amount, and do not say you will write again later. If you are past the three-month mark, send the note anyway without an elaborate apology; a late, specific note is better than a polished excuse.
How late is too late for thank-you notes?
Three months after the wedding is the usual guideline, but a late note is always better than none. Send it without a long apology.
Do we mention the amount of a cash gift?
No. Refer to what it will go towards — the home, the honeymoon, a piece of furniture — and keep the figure out of the card.
Do we need to thank guests who only attended?
Yes. A short note thanking them for celebrating with you is appropriate, especially for anyone who travelled.
